extract:
Dinosaur Jr. emerged from Amherst, Massachusetts in 1984, formed by guitarist and singer J Mascis, bassist Lou Barlow, and drummer Murph (Emmett Jefferson Murphy III). Mascis and Barlow had previously played together in the hardcore band Deep Wound, and when that group dissolved, Mascis pivoted toward something slower, heavier, and more melodic, drawing on his love of Neil Young, Black Sabbath, the Stooges, and the loud-and-tuneful template of Hüsker Dü. The band initially called itself simply Dinosaur, adding the "Jr." after a lawsuit threat from a group of veteran musicians using the same name.

Their self-titled 1985 debut on Homestead Records was a rough, eclectic introduction, but it was 1987's You're Living All Over Me, also on Homestead, that crystallized their sound: shredded ear-bleeding guitar solos, mumbled vocals, and a fragile sweetness buried under feedback. The follow-up, Bug (1988, SST Records), included the signature track "Freak Scene" and the harrowing "Don't" on which Barlow screams himself raw. Tensions between Mascis and Barlow boiled over after Bug, and Barlow was ousted, going on to form Sebadoh and later Folk Implosion. Murph and Mascis carried on, signing to Sire/Warner Bros. and releasing Green Mind in 1991, which was largely a Mascis solo effort, followed by Where You Been (1993), the band's commercial peak, which yielded the alt-rock radio staple "Start Choppin'."

Through the mid-1990s the lineup shifted around Mascis as the sole constant; Without a Sound (1994) produced the single "Feel the Pain," whose Spike Jonze-directed video became an MTV fixture during the alternative boom. By the time of Hand It Over (1997), Murph had departed and the band's commercial momentum had faded; Mascis put the project on ice and worked under his own name and with the band the Fog. Throughout this run, Dinosaur Jr. were touchstones for the indie and grunge worlds, frequently cited by Kurt Cobain and Kevin Shields as influential, and they shared scenes and bills with peers like Sonic Youth, Mudhoney, and the Pixies.

The band's most surprising act was its reunion. In 2005, Mascis, Barlow, and Murph reconvened the original lineup, signed to Merge Records, and released Beyond in 2007 — the kind of late-career return that confounded expectations by being genuinely strong rather than nostalgic. They followed it with Farm (2009), I Bet on Sky (2012), Give a Glimpse of What Yer Not (2016), and Sweep It Into Space (2021), the last co-produced with Kurt Vile. The reunited trio has now been active for longer than the original incarnation, touring consistently and releasing records at a steady clip.

Critically, Dinosaur Jr. are regarded as foundational to American indie rock and a crucial bridge between 1980s hardcore and 1990s alternative, with Mascis frequently named among the most distinctive guitarists of his generation for his Marshall-stacked, melodic, classic-rock-indebted soloing. Their early SST-era records remain canonical reference points cited by artists from My Bloody Valentine to Built to Spill to Snail Mail, and the band's unlikely second act has only solidified their reputation as one of the most durable and influential groups of the post-punk era.
title: Dinosaur Jr.
